subject: Animation
title: The Birth of Mickey Mouse
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Birth of Mickey Mouse.

hook.text: On a train ride home after losing Oswald, Walt Disney sketched a new character: a cheerful mouse.

buildup.text: Disney and Ub Iwerks designed Mickey together. Iwerks animated the first shorts at breakneck speed.

discovery.text: The third Mickey short, Steamboat Willie, featured synchronized sound and became a sensation.

twist.text: Mickey became so popular that Disney barely slept. He voiced the mouse himself for two decades.

climax.text: Mickey Mouse grew from a quick sketch into the most recognized cartoon character in history.

punchline.text: A train ride turned a stolen rabbit into a mouse empire.

quiz.question: Who co-designed and animated the first Mickey Mouse shorts?

details.summary: Mickey Mouse was created by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks in 1928 as a replacement for the lost Oswald character. Mickey's debut in Steamboat Willie, featuring synchronized sound, made him an instant sensation and launched the Disney empire.
details.whyItMatters: Mickey Mouse became the most recognizable fictional character on Earth and the foundation of a global entertainment corporation. His creation story is also a story about innovation — synchronized sound made Mickey a star.
takeaways: Mickey Mouse was created by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks in 1928
Steamboat Willie's synchronized sound made Mickey an instant sensation
Mickey became the foundation of the Walt Disney Company empire

faq.question: Who really created Mickey Mouse, Disney or Iwerks?
faq.answer: Ub Iwerks designed Mickey's visual appearance and animated the first shorts virtually alone. Walt Disney provided the voice, personality, and business vision. Mickey was a true collaboration — Iwerks drew him, but Disney made him a star.

faq.question: Why was Steamboat Willie so important?
faq.answer: It was not the first sound cartoon, but it was the first to synchronize sound effects and music precisely with animated action. Every splash, whistle, and thump matched the visuals. This integration of sound and image created an experience audiences had never seen.
